arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Sean Donahue argued the Clean Air Act requires a permit for any physical change that increases emissions.
Justice Scalia asked if the case is a regulatory interpretation question rather than a statutory one.
Justice Alito suggested that expert disagreement indicates the regulations are not clear on their face.
Chief Justice Roberts noted that agencies can change interpretations over time if rules are ambiguous.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The Clean Air Act requires owners of large pollution sources to get a permit before making changes that increase emissions. The parties disagree on how to measure those increases. Environmental Defense argues the rules require a permit for any physical change that raises output. Duke Energy argues the rules allow changes if the increase stays below a set limit.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines when power plants must get permits for upgrades. It affects how companies manage pollution controls. It shapes the balance between environmental protection and industrial flexibility. The outcome sets a standard for measuring emission increases nationwide.
